items.title: PACMAN AI framework for controlling fusion systems safely makes key decisions in milliseconds
items.excerpt: Princeton researchers built PACMAN, an AI plasma-control system that makes fusion reactor adjustments in about 20 milliseconds — far faster than a human operator. It chains multiple machine learning models to command reactor subsystems while enforcing hard safety constraints and keeping humans on the objectives.

items.title: AI automates the creation of custom functional materials atom by atom
items.excerpt: Oak Ridge National Laboratory built an AI that autonomously assembles functional materials at atomic scale, using computer vision plus reinforcement learning to move individual molecules. It constructed a 37-molecule graphene-like lattice that showed the targeted electronic properties.

items.title: AI tool detects unusual satellite behavior to improve space safety
items.excerpt: Alan Turing Institute researchers trained a model that flags abnormal satellite behavior from telescope brightness curves alone, hitting an 88% detection rate. It also separates different motion types, a step toward collision avoidance in crowded orbits.

items.title: Explainable AI could help turn hidden data patterns into testable scientific hypotheses
items.excerpt: Researchers propose a framework in which explainable-AI outputs surface model-learned patterns that scientists then test with experiments and simulations. Their core rule: a prediction is not an explanation — patterns must be validated as real physical phenomena before they inform conclusions.

items.title: Adding a 'doubt detector' helps AI optimize experiments with 40% fewer tests
items.excerpt: EPFL's GOLLuM pairs a large language model with uncertainty estimation so the system knows when it does not know. Across chemistry, materials and molecular design benchmarks it matched conventional optimization while running about 40% fewer experiments.

items.title: Researcher explores what consciousness really means—and whether it might one day emerge in a machine
items.excerpt: Neuroscientists debate whether artificial consciousness needs a biological substrate or only the right information-processing functions. The argument here is that common intuitions — such as 'biology is required' — lack empirical grounding, leaving machine consciousness genuinely unresolved.

items.title: Are We Thinking Correctly About AI Intelligence?
items.excerpt: Computer scientist Melanie Mitchell discusses why artificial intelligence doesn't 'think' or 'reason' like humans, and how we can create better methods for measuring machine cognition.

items.title: Does Computer Science Need Computers?
items.excerpt: The theoretical side of the field doesn't require computing machines. But many questions would never have been posed without them.

items.title: System helps humans predict when self-driving cars will make mistakes
items.excerpt: The CW-Net technique explains an autonomous vehicle's behavior using concepts a human can easily understand. In tests, those explanations helped drivers correctly anticipate how the vehicle would behave in surprising situations.

items.title: AI helps design new materials that work in the real world
items.excerpt: MIT researchers added a chemistry-aware component to generative materials models so the outputs are stable and practical to make. The CrysVCD approach could cut the money and time spent screening out unusable designs.

items.title: Pasqal and True Nexus Apply Quantum Computing to Protein Gelation
items.excerpt: Pasqal and True Nexus are using neutral-atom quantum computing to study protein structures linked to gelation and food protein functionality.

items.title: AI dominates the 4th International Congress of Basic Science in Beijing
items.excerpt: Subir Sarkar reports that AI was the hot topic among more than 800 delegates at Beijing's basic-science congress, from mathematics to physics sessions.

items.title: A Brain Implant in Korea Was Just Controlled From More Than 6,500 Miles Away
items.excerpt: Researchers sent commands from Chicago to a wireless brain implant in Daejeon, South Korea, 10,596 kilometers away. The demonstration suggests scientists could run and intervene in brain experiments remotely without leaving their desk.

items.title: ECG-based AI algorithm could improve detection and prediction of heart diseases
items.excerpt: Scripps Research built ECG-CLIP, a foundation model trained on 1.7 million electrocardiograms paired with clinical notes, that detects conditions such as myocardial infarction and atrial fibrillation from very few labeled examples. It outperformed existing models most clearly in low-data settings.

items.title: AI-designed “intrabodies” could unlock new treatments for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and MND
items.excerpt: Researchers developed a new way to turn ordinary antibodies into tiny disease-fighting molecules that can work inside human cells, potentially opening new paths for treating Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's disease, and motor neurone disease.
